name: Lena Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get the apprentice to lay the tester out before we leave the yard. I'm 27, but I lead the repair crew and hold a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence. Homes and little shops are most of our calls; I like finding the fault everyone else missed. The pay is low and my savings cover less than three weeks, so I ride an old scooter to keep rent covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the apprentice to put the phone away and check the circuit again. An app saving five minutes won't mend a loose connection behind a cupboard. I'd rather the firm paid for decent test leads than another subscription.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands feel useful in that picture, but my bank account still frightens me. I'm 27 with a master's licence and less than three weeks of expenses put by. The licence doesn't make my employer pay well, and there aren't many other firms close enough to reach on my old scooter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the repair jobs and checking the apprentice's work myself. From next payday I'll stop buying lunch and put the saved 20 a week in a separate account. Through the first year I'd keep those same habits rather than buy software I don't want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm worried about an ordinary bad month, not about a clever computer. A broken scooter would put me in difficulty even with the same work coming in. Knowing the job still needs me helps me sleep a bit better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes buying lunch worth changing first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bakery bag is small enough that I pretend it doesn't count. Five bags a week count when I add them on paper. I can make sandwiches without asking anybody for a favour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would notice if you were struggling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My older brother Pavel would notice the scooter sitting outside when I should be at work. I'd ask my brother for a lift before I'd ask for money. We were raised to help family get to work, not to pretend everything is fine.

say: I'd tell the **apprentice** to check the circuit rather than trust a phone.
I'd rather the firm bought **test leads** than another software subscription.
think: My **licence** keeps me useful, but low pay still leaves almost no spare money.
I have fewer than **three weeks** saved and few nearby employers I could reach.
do: Keep **leading repairs** and checking the apprentice's work through the first year.
Pack **lunch** and save the resulting 20 each week from next payday.
feel: **Anxious** about a broken scooter interrupting an otherwise useful working life.
S0.quote: A broken scooter would put me in difficulty even with the same work coming in.
fieldNote: Her **master's licence** provides occupational confidence without a financial cushion; qualifications have not delivered better local bargaining options.
She names a small **lunch saving** she controls and a family lift before considering any request for cash.

steps.text: Keep leading home and business repair jobs
Save 20 weekly by bringing lunch from home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let the office try faster booking, but don't promise customers a shorter safety check. A repair isn't finished because a screen says the next appointment has started. The apprentice would hear that from me twice if necessary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office work could get cheaper before anything changes inside a wall. I worry the owner would squeeze another call into our day and call the extra pressure progress. I might lose paid hours if faster planning means fewer quiet gaps, though I don't expect the repair work to vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month I'll write down the time each safety check actually takes, including trips to isolate the power. In the first year I'd take that notebook to the owner before agreeing to a fuller route. I'll also drop my paid film subscription now so a short week hurts less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel pushed from somewhere I can't see. My own tools haven't changed, yet I could still end up running faster for less money. Keeping a record gives me something firmer than an argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the booking software yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the office to print my route as usual. I've never used AI and I don't want to learn on a customer's job. If a slot is impossible, I'll ring the office and explain why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the owner about one crowded day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Tuesday a kitchen repair needed another isolation check because the labels were wrong. I'd show the owner that exact job and the extra forty minutes. I'd rather lose an argument over a timetable than hurry an apprentice through a dangerous board.

say: I'd accept faster **booking** only if the firm kept enough time for safe checks.
I'd remind the **apprentice** that a full diary doesn't mean a repair is finished.
think: I worry **planning software** could squeeze more calls into the same working day.
My **paid hours** could shrink even while homes still need hands to repair wiring.
do: Record **checking times** now and discuss crowded routes with the owner during the first year.
Cancel my **film subscription** now to reduce the cost of a short working week.
feel: **Anxious** about lower earnings and pressure to hurry work that still needs careful hands.
S1.quote: My own tools haven't changed, yet I could still end up running faster for less money.
fieldNote: She separates **office automation** from physical repair rather than assuming a robot immediately replaces her on site.
Her resistance appears as a preference for **printed routes** and evidence from familiar work, not an invented technical workaround.

steps.text: Keep repair work documented when discussing crowded routes with the owner
Cancel the paid film subscription this month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the apprentice there are still wires to pull before 2031. I'd also say a trade is worth doing properly even when people boast that machines will do everything. I wouldn't tell a young worker that a licence is a promise for life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking part arrives in 2028, but I hear the 2031 date more loudly because that's when capable robots come. I expect my income to take a big hit if the firm can eventually send a machine to do the ordinary installations. I lie awake imagining my tools still in the box and no call coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd end the scooter replacement plan and keep repairing the one I have. I'd ask my brother this month whether I could use his spare room if my income fell. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep taking paid repair calls, but move in with him only if reduced hours made my rent impossible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened enough to rehearse the conversation with my brother. I can still make a plan, but I hate needing a room I haven't paid for. The three years before robots would be time to earn, not proof that I'm safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your brother's room be an agreed fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not until I actually ask my brother and get an answer. I'd explain the rent figure and offer to pay for food and electricity while I was working. I won't write free housing into my sums just because we're related.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What work would you expect in that first year after 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Faults in older homes would still need somebody to trace cables and open things carefully. I'd take that work while the physical tasks remain, even if the office uses a powerful system to arrange calls. I'm not assuming the system leaves our prices alone.

say: I'd tell the **apprentice** physical wiring still needs people before robots arrive around 2031.
I wouldn't promise that a **licence** protects anyone's whole working life.
think: I expect **robot installations** could eventually take a large part of my income.
I already lose **sleep** imagining the repair phone falling silent with almost no savings behind me.
do: Cancel the **scooter replacement** plan now and maintain my current scooter.
Ask my **brother** about a spare room, using it after 2028 only if reduced hours make rent unaffordable.
Keep taking **paid repairs** in the first year after thinking AI arrives.
feel: **Alarmed** about a large income loss, with an uncomfortable family fallback still needing agreement.
S2.quote: The three years before robots would be time to earn, not proof that I'm safe.
fieldNote: Her expected **income loss** is tied to later physical automation, while the first post-2028 year still contains hands-on repair work.
The proposed **family room** remains conditional on consent and unaffordable rent; no free housing or guaranteed support is assumed.

steps.text: Cancel plans to replace the scooter
Ask brother about temporary housing if reduced hours make rent unaffordable after 2028
Keep accepting paid repair calls in the first post-2028 year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives an apprentice time to finish learning before the thinking systems arrive. That's better than the two-year rush. I'd still be honest that robots following around 2034 could change the value of the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes a difference to my savings, not to whether a machine can eventually compete with me. I could reach 2031 with a little room to refuse a bad offer if I start now. My own hours could still shrink, so I'd be anxious rather than comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owner next week for a pay review using the repair jobs I already lead as evidence. If a rise came, I'd put the whole increase into my separate savings account; without a rise I'd keep the lunch saving. In the first year after 2031 I'd stay with paid repairs and review the account each month before accepting fewer hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less trapped when I can count five years of small deposits. I'm still cross that a master electrician has to build security one sandwich at a time. I wouldn't pretend the pay rise has already happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to that pay meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the list of repair jobs I led without a return visit and the apprentice checks I signed. I'd ask for a fixed increase, not praise in front of the van. The owner could say no; there aren't many local firms for me to threaten to join.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes if the answer is no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I keep the same lunch saving and the old scooter. I don't book a course or sign a new rental agreement on money I haven't got. Five years helps only if I actually keep the deposits going.

say: I'd say **five years** gives the apprentice more time to learn before thinking AI arrives.
I'd still warn that **robots around 2034** could change what electrical skills earn.
think: I could build enough **savings** to refuse a bad offer by 2031 if I start now.
My **hours** could still shrink, and more preparation time doesn't remove eventual competition.
do: Request a **pay review** next week with evidence from repair jobs I lead.
Save any **pay increase**, or keep the lunch saving if the owner refuses.
Continue **paid repairs** and review savings monthly during the first year after 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, but less trapped because five years permits repeated small deposits.
S3.quote: I'm still cross that a master electrician has to build security one sandwich at a time.
fieldNote: Her **pay request** rests on existing responsibilities rather than an unsupported assumption that local employers will compete for her.
The **saving plan** explicitly excludes a pay rise until agreed; familiar work remains her preferred response to uncertainty.

steps.text: Save any agreed pay rise or continue saving 20 weekly from lunches
Keep paid repairs and review savings monthly after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to plan like an adult rather than run at the last minute. I still want young people learning a trade, with honest warnings about what might change. Nobody should sell an apprenticeship as a lifetime guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37 when thinking AI arrived and about 40 when the robots followed, so retirement isn't the answer. Repair work looks steady over the next few years, but a broken scooter could still interrupt my earnings before I build cash. Ten years helps with the later threat; it doesn't fill my account tonight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the lunch saving now and take the pay evidence to the owner as in the five-year picture. I'd put any agreed increase aside too, rather than upgrade my scooter just because the threat feels distant. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep doing paid fault repairs and check actual hours before changing my housing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the next repair bill, but I have more room to breathe about AI than in the fast picture. I don't suddenly fancy using AI because the date is farther away. I like having years in which being careful with familiar things might be enough for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop the decade slipping away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mark the savings balance on the first page of my paper diary every month. My brother could ask me about that number when we have Sunday lunch. I wouldn't ask him to police my spending, just to stop me forgetting my own plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could fault repair protect you once robots arrive around 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and I wouldn't advertise myself as impossible to replace. Old buildings are awkward, but a capable robot could learn awkward work too. The point of saving is to have choices if my confidence about repairs turns out wrong.

say: I'd call **ten years** useful preparation time while refusing to promise apprentices lifetime security.
I'd still encourage **trade learning** when the uncertainty is explained honestly at the start.
think: I expect steady **repair work**, but a broken scooter could still interrupt earnings before I've built more cash.
I'll only be about **40** when robots arrive, so retirement cannot solve the longer problem.
do: Keep the **lunch saving** now and save any agreed pay rise instead of upgrading my scooter.
Record the **savings balance** monthly in my paper diary.
Continue **paid fault repairs** after 2036 and check actual hours before changing housing.
feel: **Anxious** about an immediate repair bill, with more breathing room to prepare for later automation.
S4.quote: The point of saving is to have choices if my confidence about repairs turns out wrong.
fieldNote: The **ten-year horizon** softens automation fears without erasing present transport and savings risks or her resistant attitude to technology.
She rejects assumed **retirement** and admits physical repair may also be automated, preserving the common AGI endpoint across timelines.

steps.text: Continue lunch savings and save any agreed pay increase
Keep paid fault repair work after 2036 while checking actual hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I'd expect a serious income loss when the robots follow, without enough time to build cash. A written, honest work forecast from the owner would help, along with a pay review based on the jobs I lead. If things went badly, I'd ask my brother about temporary housing, but he would have to agree.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether keeping the job also means keeping enough paid hours. I can still own a full toolbox and have an empty food cupboard. I don't want anyone telling the apprentice that being good guarantees being paid.

headlineQuote: I can still own a full toolbox and have an empty food cupboard.
portrait: Lena is **27**, leads repair work, and holds a technical diploma and master's licence despite low pay and very little savings.
She trusts **familiar methods**, checks apprentices closely, and prefers paper records to AI tools she has never used.
A short timetable brings **family fallback** planning, while longer timetables let her pursue pay recognition and small regular savings.
Her **confidence in repair** is limited: she expects useful hands-on work before robots, without claiming protection once capable robots arrive.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves too little saving time before she expects a serious income loss when robots follow.
whatWouldHelp: An honest **work forecast** and a pay review reflecting the repair jobs she leads would help.
Temporary **family housing** could help if her brother agrees and reduced hours make rent unaffordable.
